title: Microbes and the stages from carriage to illness
audience: Cleaning and support workers in healthcare settings such as aged care, medical and dental clinics and NDIS services, with no clinical training.
learningOutcomes: Sort a listed organism into bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites using its description.
Explain how carrying a microbe differs from being infected or unwell, with one example of each.
Explain why a product that works on bacteria may not work on a spore-forming organism.

instruction.heading: Microbes are not all alike
instruction.body: Microorganisms are too small to see with the eye alone. The ones that matter in a care setting fall into four broad families: bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Protozoa are single-celled organisms that behave like parasites, so they are usually grouped with them. The families differ in how they multiply, how they survive on a surface and how they respond to cleaning products. You do not need a laboratory background to use this. What counts is knowing that a method suited to one family may fail against another, and that the facility product list, not a guess, decides what you use.

instruction.heading: Bacteria, spores and the limits of disinfectants
instruction.body: A bacterium is a single-celled organism without a nucleus. Many bacteria are killed by a properly applied disinfectant spray or wipe. Some bacteria can form spores, a dormant and tough form that tolerates heat, drying and many chemicals. Spores are the main reason a surface can look clean and still carry a risk. Destroying spores in general requires sterilisation, which happens in controlled equipment such as an autoclave and is not a cleaning task. Chemical disinfectants that kill bacteria will not reliably kill their spores. Where the facility names a spore-forming organism, use the product it lists for that organism and no other.

instruction.heading: Viruses need a living host
instruction.body: A virus cannot multiply by itself. It enters living cells and uses them to make new copies. Inside, it carries genetic material wrapped in a protein shell, and some viruses also carry an outer envelope that helps them attach to cells. Enveloped viruses tend to respond more readily to cleaning products than viruses without an envelope, which is why product choice matters (the product rules are in “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals”, and the envelope point is in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”). For you, the practical point is that a virus left on a surface can be picked up by the hands, so surface cleaning and hand hygiene belong together.

instruction.heading: Carriage, infection and illness are separate stages
instruction.body: Microbes can live on or in a person without causing harm. When they multiply but no signs appear, the person is colonised, and a colonised person can still pass organisms to others. That is why standard cleaning applies to every person and not only to those who look unwell. Infection begins when microbes start to damage cells, usually with local signs such as pain, swelling or redness. Disease follows when the damage disturbs normal body function and the person feels unwell. The three stages differ, and a person can move between them. Your role is to treat every person and every body fluid as a possible source, and to refer any sign of infection to the nurse in charge.

instruction.heading: What decides whether infection takes hold
instruction.body: The learner guide names three factors: how many harmful organisms get into the body, how quickly the organism can reproduce, and how strong the body defences are. Your work affects the first factor directly. Cleaning reduces the number of organisms in the environment, hand hygiene limits how many reach a person, and correct cleaning stops organisms building up in soiled places. Damp buildings can grow fungi that cleaning alone does not resolve. Visible mould is outside this lesson and falls under the high-risk cleaning module, which has its own controls and warnings.

procedure: Before starting an area, read the cleaning schedule and note any organism named there or any sign of infection that the nurse in charge has reported.
Sort each concern into bacteria, virus, fungus or parasite. If you cannot sort it, ask your supervisor before choosing a method.
Check that the product you plan to use is listed for that concern, either on its label or on the facility list.
If a person shows redness, swelling, pain or discharge, do not diagnose it. Tell the nurse in charge and note the referral.
Record any organism concern you were given, the time, and the person you passed it to.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner in a dental clinic is told that a child had a skin rash while sitting in a treatment chair an hour earlier.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should happen before the chair is wiped?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not decide what the rash is. Put on gloves, check the facility list for the product for that surface, and ask the nurse whether any further step applies. Note the referral in your log.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner must clean a bathroom where a patient has had a bowel accident. The room sign names an organism that forms spores.
workedExamples.reasoning: Probably not. Spores resist many disinfectants, so use the product the facility lists for that organism and follow its label. Ask the supervisor if the list is unclear. Wear the protective items the spill procedure requires (see “Managing spills of body fluid at work”).

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves for any task involving body fluid or a contaminated surface
Facility product list, or the label of the product being used

commonErrors.error: Judging an organism by how harmless it looks, or judging a surface by how clean it appears.
commonErrors.prevention: Visible cleanliness does not show whether microbes are present. Use the method for the item every time.

commonErrors.error: Using a product that is only listed for bacteria when the concern is a spore-forming organism.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the facility list for that organism before choosing a product.

commonErrors.error: Diagnosing a person from the look of a skin mark or a discharge.
commonErrors.prevention: Pass the sign on to the nurse in charge and do not discuss it with others.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not diagnose or speculate about a person condition. Share concerns only with the nurse in charge or the infection prevention team.
Visible mould is outside this lesson. It is handled under the high-risk cleaning module with its own controls and warnings.

They have not been checked against an Australian microbiology text. The spore and enveloped-virus product points are cross-checked against “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”, which reworks the NHMRC guideline.

qualityStandard: Learner names the four microbe families and says which of them can form spores.
Learner explains carriage, infection and illness in their own words, with one example of each.
Learner states why a product listed for bacteria may not be suitable for a spore-forming organism.
documentationEvidence: Log entry naming any organism concern that was passed on, and the person it was passed to.
summary: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites differ in how they multiply and how they respond to products.
Carriage, infection and illness are separate stages, and a carrier can still pass organisms on.
A spore-forming organism needs the product the facility lists for it, not a general spray.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which microbe family is a single-celled organism without a nucleus?
A person carries a microbe on the skin, the microbe multiplies, and the person has no symptoms. Which term describes this?
Why might a general disinfectant that kills bacteria still leave a risk on a surface?
options: Such products rarely touch bacteria on the surface at all
Some bacteria form spores, which resist many disinfectants.
Spores grow only in water, so wiping is enough.
Viruses are immune to all cleaning methods.
